## Hard-to-vary report: Lucretius, *Of the Nature of Things* (Book I, with the Book II proem and atomic motions)

**1. The question, frozen**

The document answers several questions. The one its title and opening make central is: **what is everything made of, and by what law do things come to be and pass away?** Range: the whole sum of things, everywhere, for all time ("the unmeasurable All"). Kind of question: mostly *what produces it*, plus two *why can it not happen* blocks — nothing from nothing, nothing to nothing. Parked, because they are separate claims: why motion is possible (already inside the above), whether the universe is bounded, what makes life bearable (Book II proem). Freeze these; changing one makes a new claim.

**2. The explanation in parts** (author's words)

P1 "Nothing from nothing ever yet was born"; "naught perishes ever to annihilation."
P2 "Primal germs" — solid, "without a void", eternal, fixed shapes, "minimums of nature".
P3 "There's in things a void" — "place intangible", imponderable.
P4 All nature "consists of twain of things: of bodies and of void."
P5 Things are unions; qualities come from "clashings, motions, order, posture, shapes".
P6 The swerve: atoms "decline a little."
P7 Infinite sum and void; no bottom, no centre, "no rest".
P8 Properties against accidents: "time exists not of itself"; Helen and Troy are accidents of body and place.
P9 Gods take no hand in it; Venus, Mars, the Muse, Memmius.

**3. Part by part**

| Part | Mark | Held by / note |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Held | The seed, season, slow-growth and cultivation jobs all break without it. Caution below |
| P2 | Held | Motion, weight and kind-constancy break without something solid and changeless. Its minimums are **held if** — held only by "no half-of-half forever", which is argued, not observed |
| P3 | Held | Remove it and motion dies *and* equal-sized weights come out equal. The strongest part |
| P4 | Not a separate part | It restates P2 + P3. Counting it again adds nothing |
| P5 | Held | This is the workings, not the outputs (look-inside passes). Each specific quality-claim is looser |
| P6 | Held if | Its only jobs are "no fixed fate" and free will — doubts you added. No change distinguishes swerved from straight atoms: no gauge |
| P7 | Held | The thrown spear is a block argument: any edge can be passed. Infinite matter follows less tightly |
| P8 | Held | "Had been no matter, and no room", no war: the flip is covered |
| P9a Venus/Mars/Muse/Memmius | Idle | Decoration for this question. He says himself the germs "did not make a compact" |
| P9b No gods in the workings | Held | Removing it removes the poem's point |

**4. Whole-explanation checks**

- **Flip.** Had things come from nothing, he says we would see sudden births in alien months and men from the sea. He would have been caught. Good.
- **Reverse.** He is running forward: poke the seeds and the thing moves; poke the thing and the seeds do not. Correct direction.
- **Hunt.** Careful here: P1 is used to prove P2, and P2 to prove P1. That is a loop. It is rescued because each side also leans on separate jobs (seasons, growth, rain, weight, motion) — say so, and keep it visible.
- **Where the jobs came from.** All given by the author. The jobs "free will exists" (P6) and "no infinite division" (P2) are the doubtful ones.
- **Pull.** P2 and P5 pull: solid, voidless atoms against soft, penetrable things. He draws the line between atoms and unions. What would show the line misplaced: an atom cut, bent or wetted. That is checkable in principle, so the line is honestly drawn.
- **Patches and catch-alls.** P6 is the patch: a minimum "some other cause of motion" added to absorb free will and to start collisions. No gauge is offered for it. This is the loosest thing in the poem.
- **Rivals.** Excellent. He swaps atoms for fire, for the four elements, for Anaxagoras' seeds-that-look-like-things, and shows each fails a job. This is what makes the book hard to vary, and it also shows the *really* held part is more general than "atoms": **an unchanging stuff that stays put while arrangement, order and motion produce the variety.**
- **Change list left out.** He says plainly up front that eyes cannot see germs, and argues by inference instead. That limit is stated, not slipped in. Not covered here: the senses, the soul, how we come to know.
- **Where parts came from.** *Built:* the void (argued from motion and weight), the refutation of rivals, the arrangement-mechanism. *Fitted:* the seasons and kind-constancy, matched to many past cases. *Asserted:* the swerve, the senses as final court, the reality of unseen germs.
- **Warning.** The sunbeam mites read like evidence but are an analogy. A picture that fits is not a test.

**5. What would make it harder to vary**

1. Give the swerve a gauge: name one thing we could look at that would differ if atoms never swerved. Without it P6 is a placeholder.
2. Break the P1/P2 loop: say which jobs hold "nothing from nothing" alone.

**6. What this does not show**

Passing does not make it true; the atoms could be wrong and still hard to vary. The rival-sweep is the part to trust; the swerve and the gods-talk are the parts to doubt.

**7. One next step**

Take the two halves of one poke he already gives: if heavier bodies fell faster and did not swerve, what would we see? He answers "no creation". Ask for the observation that would show the answer — and if none exists, mark it unknown.
